_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03). Chaque piste est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: At Kong, it was said in the late 1880s that the Daou families, like the Ouattara, the Barou, the Kérou and the Touré, had come from the north, from the region of Ségou and Djenné, in small groups and not in a single migration. One of the town's seven quarters bore their name: Daoura, "the quarter of the Daou".
oralTraditions.collector: Louis-Gustave Binger, officier et explorateur français, arrivé à Kong en février 1888
oralTraditions.context: Information gathered at Kong, in present-day Côte d'Ivoire, from informants whom he does not name, and published in French in 1892 in his travel narrative

oralTraditions.claim: The same narrative makes the Daou one of the Mande-Dioula families that first settled at Ténenguéra, near Kong, with the Ouattara and the Barou. Allied with the Ouattara led by Sékou, and in collusion with the Kouroubari, the Daou and the Barou are said to have taken Kong by surprise on a major market day, massacred the Falafalla chiefs and replaced the power of the first inhabitants with their own.
oralTraditions.collector: Louis-Gustave Binger, officier et explorateur français
oralTraditions.context: Narrative gathered at Kong in 1888 and 1889 and published in French in 1892

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary or study consulted gives a meaning for the word. The dictionary of Mandinka clan names defines Dawu only as a clan name, and the 1892 narrative that names the Daou of Kong offers no explanation of it.

The name is written in several ways. The dictionary of Mandinka clan names gives Dawu, with the variant Dawo, and places it among the Minyanka, around Sikasso and Ségou; a 2015 Malian report cites Dao among Minyanka family names, with Goïta, Dembélé and Sogoba; the 1892 travel narrative writes Daou for the families of Kong. None of these sources says that these forms designate one and the same lineage.

A historian rereading the 1892 narrative in 2000 classes Daou among the Bambara clan names of Kong, apparently from the region of Ségou and San. This is his interpretation: the 1892 narrative speaks of Mande-Dioula families from the region of Ségou and Djenné, and does not name San.

The explorer who visited Kong in 1888 translates the name of the Daoura quarter as "the quarter of the Daou", explaining that -ra means "of the" there. It is the name of the quarter that he explains, not that of the clan.

casteOrSocialFunction.value: The dictionary of Mandinka clan names links Dawu to the jeli, the griots, but itself marks this status with a question mark. No other source consulted confirms or contradicts it.

homonyms.label: Dao (nom vietnamien)
homonyms.distinction: The same word is written Dao in Vietnam, where it is borne by far more people than in West Africa. We have found no source linking the two names, and nothing indicates that they are related.

homonyms.label: Daw (Ndaw)
homonyms.distinction: The dictionary of Mandinka clan names gives a separate entry, Daw, with the variants Ndaw and Dafe, borne notably among the Wolof, the Fulani, the Toucouleur and the Marka. It does not link it to Dawu, the name borne among the Minyanka, and we have found no source that links the two.

sources.title: Autoportrait du Mali — Les Obstacles à la Paix
sources.notes: Action-research report by the Malian Institute for Action Research for Peace with Interpeace, in partnership with the United Nations, March 2015. Its chapter on sociocultural diversity (p. 26) gives, for each major group in Mali, a few family names, often followed by "etc.": Dao appears among the Minyanka names, with Goïta, Dembélé and Sogoba. The list is illustrative, with no stated method of compilation or source. It attests that a name is borne in a group, not where it comes from.

sources.title: Dao — origine, signification et incidence du nom de famille
sources.notes: Global genealogy aggregator, consulted on 29 September 2026. Worldwide incidence of about 835,374 bearers; Vietnam 593,679, Mali 97,834, Burkina Faso 74,123, Côte d'Ivoire 27,803, United States 12,287. The page gives no meaning for the name. The figures outside Africa are not included in the attestations of this fiche.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, the electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), noted by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The Dawu entry gives the variant Dawo, the Minyanka group, the regions of Sikasso and Ségou, and the jeli status followed by a question mark; it gives no meaning for the name, no equivalent, and no joking partner. The separate entry Daw gives the variants Ndaw and Dafe, among the Wolof, the Fulani, the Toucouleur and the Marka, among others. A 2017 dissertation on the clan names of the Manden repeats the Dawu entry without adding anything.

sources.title: Du Niger au golfe de Guinée par le pays de Kong et le Mossi
sources.notes: Binger, Louis-Gustave, Hachette, Paris, 1892, two volumes; digital reissue by Project Gutenberg (volume 2: https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/74721), which keeps the printed pagination. The author is a French officer on an exploration mission from 1887 to 1889, preparing colonial expansion: he is cited for what he was told at Kong, not for his classifications, and he himself writes that he found no written record of this history at Kong (p. 323). Volume 1: arrival at Kong, noted for Monday 20 February in his journal (p. 284), and Bafotigué Daou put at his service (p. 291); the house of Fotigué Daou, with whom he lodges, on the plan of the town, and the Daoura quarter among the seven quarters (p. 294); Daoura, "quarter of the Daou", and its indigo dye pits (p. 297); the Daou among the families said to have come from the region of Ségou and Djenné (p. 323); the Barou and the Daou allied with the Ouattara in the capture of Kong (p. 324). Volume 2: Bafotigué Daou accompanies the author on his departure from Kong, on 21 January 1889, and the Ouattara, Barou and Daou families come from Ténenguéra (p. 208).

sources.title: The Wangara, an Old Soninke Diaspora in West Africa?
sources.notes: Massing, Andreas, Cahiers d'Études africaines, 158, XL-2, 2000, pp. 281-308; full text in open access, consulted on 3 October 2026. Paragraph 58 (p. 298 of the printed edition) classes the Daou, with the Baro, Balo, Cissé and Touré, among the Bambara clan names of Kong that came, apparently, from the region of Ségou and San. His note 38 cites Binger's travel narrative published in 1892, but cuts out its mention of Djenné; the 1892 narrative, moreover, places the Sissé in another group. The article deals with the Soninke diaspora and not with the name Dao alone: this is an incidental passage.

gaps.reason: We have found no chronicle or writing by an author from these societies that speaks of the origin of this name.

We do not know whether this name, among the Minyanka, is a clan name of local origin or an adopted Mandinka clan name. Nor do we know whether the Daou of Kong and the Minyanka Dawu form a single lineage: the Daou of Kong are said to have come from the region of Ségou, where the dictionary also places Dawu, but no source consulted links them.

The sources do not agree on the people of the Daou of Kong: the 1892 narrative counts them among the Mande-Dioula families, while a historian in 2000 makes it a Bambara clan name. In Burkina Faso, where the name is borne by more than seventy thousand people, we have found no source that links it to a people.
The dictionary of Mandinka clan names gives no joking partner for this name, and we have found none elsewhere.
No source consulted says how this name is transmitted among those who bear it.
